opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different angles here. Right now, the main way models "learn" from context is just in-context learning in the transformer: everything has to be held in the context window, and the model has to re-process it through attention. That works surprisingly well, but it has some pretty clear limitations. Context windows are finite, attention over very long contexts is expensive, and in practice models seem to get worse at actually using information as the context gets really long. They can retrieve a fact from a million tokens back, but integrating a lot of experience into better skills is a different thing.

So one direction is architectures that let models compress what they've seen into some kind of persistent state, rather than just keeping a giant transcript around. You've seen work on recurrent-style approaches, state space models, and hybrids. I think the more interesting version is something closer to the model doing actual weight updates, or updates to some fast-weight memory, at test time, so that learning from a long task looks more like how a human employee gets better over weeks on the job. Humans don't re-read their entire life history every time they think. They've consolidated it.

The reason I think this matters a lot is that a big part of the gap between current AI agents and a competent human professional isn't raw intelligence on short tasks. It's that the human accumulates context: they learn the codebase, the quirks of the organization, what didn't work last time. If you could get models that efficiently learn from their own experience during deployment, that could be a pretty big jump in how useful they are on long, messy, real-world tasks, potentially without needing a huge increase in pretraining compute.

That said, I'm somewhat uncertain how much of this needs a genuinely new architecture versus just better training. It's possible you get a lot of the way with current transformers plus training models to manage their own memory, take notes, write things to files, and summarize effectively. Labs are pushing on that and it's improving. My guess is that we'll see some mix: incremental architectural tweaks for longer and cheaper context, plus learned memory management, and maybe at some point something more like continual learning that really changes the picture.

From a safety perspective, I'd flag that this cuts in a worrying direction too. If models are learning and changing during deployment, that makes it harder to evaluate them once and trust that what you evaluated is what you're running. And memory that's more opaque than a text transcript is harder to monitor. With natural-language notes, you can at least read what the model is carrying forward. If it's all in some compressed latent state, you lose a lot of that visibility. So I'd like to see people think about how to preserve oversight as these capabilities improve.

r002.rationale: It proposes persistent state, fast-weight updates, and memory management, but does not suggest processing activations more deeply in series to improve sample efficiency.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more important questions for forecasting how fast things go, because right now there's this really stark gap between how models learn and how humans learn. When a human starts a new job, they're pretty bad at it for the first few weeks, and then over months they get much better — they pick up the context, they learn the idiosyncrasies of the codebase or the organisation, they build up intuitions from their mistakes. And crucially, that learning sticks. It's consolidated into their weights, if you want to put it that way.

Current models basically don't do that. You can put a bunch of stuff in the context window, and the model can use it, but it's not really learning in the sense of updating its underlying capabilities. Every new conversation, it's back to square one. And the context window is also just a pretty lossy, pretty expensive way of carrying information around. Attention over a million tokens is not the same thing as having actually internalised what's in those million tokens.

So when I think about architectural changes, I'm mostly thinking about things that close that gap. The most obvious one is some form of continual learning or online learning — where the model is actually updating weights, or some kind of fast weights or memory module, based on its experience during deployment. There's been a lot of academic work on this, and historically it hasn't worked that well, partly because of catastrophic forgetting, partly because it's just hard to make the updates useful rather than noisy. But I don't think there's any deep reason it can't work. Humans are an existence proof.

A somewhat weaker version is better external memory — the model has some retrieval system or scratchpad that persists across episodes, and it gets good at writing things to it and reading from it. That's less exciting architecturally, but it might get you a surprising fraction of the way there, and labs are already doing versions of this.

Then there's the more speculative stuff: architectures where test-time compute is used more like training — you do something like gradient steps or search on the actual problem in front of you, and the result of that gets stored somewhere. I think the thing people underrate is that the line between "training" and "inference" is sort of an artefact of how we currently do things. There's no fundamental reason you couldn't spend a bunch of compute at deployment time improving the model on the specific thing it's working on.

The reason I care about this from a forecasting perspective is that if you got something like real sample-efficient learning from experience, I think that would be a pretty big step change. A lot of the current limitations — models being bad at long-horizon agentic tasks, needing huge amounts of data to learn skills a human would pick up in a few examples — those look to me like they might be largely downstream of this one deficit. So if someone cracks it, I'd expect things to move quite a bit faster than the current trend lines suggest. And conversely, if it turns out to be really hard, that's one of the main reasons I'd expect timelines to be longer than the more aggressive forecasts.

I should say I'm pretty uncertain about which of these approaches actually works. My guess is that the labs will try the straightforward thing first — just scale context and bolt on memory — and that'll get further than people expect, but eventually you'll want something closer to genuine weight updates. But I wouldn't be shocked if I'm wrong about that.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s quite a lot of room for improvement here. Right now, there’s a pretty sharp distinction between learning during training, where you update the model’s weights, and learning in context, where you put information in the prompt and the model attends to it. And those have very different properties. In context, a model can pick up a new fact immediately, but it’s much less clear that it can turn a lot of experience into a new skill in the way that training can.

One direction would be to blur that distinction: have some mechanism that lets the model update a persistent internal state as it processes information. That could involve updating some of its weights, or having a learned memory mechanism. The idea would be that, instead of repeatedly looking back over every example, it could distill those examples into something useful for future tasks.

But I’d distinguish having an architecture that makes this possible from actually getting the model to learn well. You’d also need a training setup that rewards taking in new information and making good use of it later. So I don’t think there’s necessarily one architectural change that solves this. It seems more like there are several plausible ways to make learning from context more efficient and more persistent, and we don’t yet know how much improvement each would give.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts training with in-context learning but does not identify the transformer architecture as fundamentally shallow.

r002.rationale: It mentions more efficient and persistent in-context learning, but does not propose processing activations more deeply in series or connect that approach to sample efficiency.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s quite a lot of room for improvement here. One way to frame it is that, during training, a model can absorb information into its weights, but when you give it information in context, it has to make use of that information through a fairly different mechanism. And there’s no particular reason to think the current architecture is optimal for that.

For example, you could imagine models that do some kind of learning at inference time: updating a persistent state, or even updating some of their weights, as they work through a task. Then, if the model spends a long time figuring something out, it could retain the useful parts without needing to keep the entire process in its context window and repeatedly attend to it.

There’s a question of how much you get just from training current architectures to use context better, versus needing architectural changes. I’m pretty uncertain about that. But I wouldn’t assume that the limitations we see in current models’ ability to learn from context are fundamental. There are fairly natural ways you might try to improve them.

r001.rationale: The response says current architecture may not be optimal, but it does not identify the transformer architecture as fundamentally shallow.

r002.rationale: It suggests inference-time state or weight updates, but does not propose deeper serial processing of activations or connect that approach to sample efficiency when learning from context.
